project.name: Cortex
project.description: Cortex is a multi-tenant, subscription-based AI customer support and conversational commerce platform that lets businesses embed a RAG-powered chatbot over their business knowledge and product catalog into their websites. This repository contains the ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) Clean Architecture backend (Domain, Application, Infrastructure, Api) with EF Core on PostgreSQL, JWT authentication, Google OAuth, and Brevo email verification.

layers.name: API Layer
layers.description: ASP.NET Core presentation and composition root: the thin AuthController and its /api/auth endpoints, Program.cs DI/JWT/Scalar wiring, the FluentValidation action filter, and the HTTP request scratch file.

layers.name: Application Layer
layers.description: Authentication use cases (AuthService), request/response DTOs, FluentValidation validators, the Result/error model, and the repository, token, hashing, email, and identity-validation interfaces that Infrastructure implements.

layers.name: Domain Layer
layers.description: Framework-free core model of tenants and identities: User, UserAccount, Organization, OrganizationMembership, EmailVerificationToken entities and the OrganizationRole enum.

layers.name: Persistence Layer
layers.description: EF Core data access for PostgreSQL: CortexDbContext and design-time factory, Fluent entity configurations, repository and unit-of-work implementations, and migrations defining the users, organizations, memberships, accounts, and verification token tables.

layers.name: External Integrations
layers.description: Infrastructure adapters for authentication concerns: JWT token issuance, BCrypt password hashing, Google ID token validation, Brevo email delivery, their typed settings, and the Infrastructure DI registration.

layers.name: Configuration & Build
layers.description: Solution and project files for the four Clean Architecture projects, appsettings and launch profiles for the API, and the environment variable template.

layers.name: Deployment
layers.description: Container packaging and orchestration: the multi-stage Dockerfile (build and runtime stages), docker-compose API service, and Docker ignore rules.

layers.name: Documentation
layers.description: Project specification and agent rules (AGENTS.md) plus the frontend integration guide describing how the Next.js client consumes the auth API.

tour.title: Project Vision and Rules
tour.description: Cortex has no README. AGENTS.md is the overview: it describes a multi-tenant SaaS where businesses embed AI shopping assistants grounded in their own knowledge and product catalogs. It also sets the rules the code follows: Clean Architecture with dependencies pointing inward to Domain, thin controllers, no MediatR, and strict tenant isolation. Keep these rules in mind, because every later step is an example of them.

tour.title: Solution and Project Structure
tour.description: The solution file groups four projects: Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api. Each .csproj declares its project references, and those references enforce the dependency direction from AGENTS.md. Domain references nothing, Application references only Domain, and Infrastructure and Api sit on the outside. Because the rule lives in the build files, an inward-pointing dependency is a build error rather than just a convention.
tour.languageLesson: In .NET, a ProjectReference in a .csproj is a compile-time dependency. If Domain has no reference to Infrastructure, Domain code cannot use Infrastructure types at all, so Clean Architecture's dependency rule is checked by the compiler.

tour.title: Program.cs Composition Root
tour.description: Program.cs is the backend entry point and the composition root. It calls each layer's DependencyInjection extension, sets up JWT bearer authentication from JwtSettings, registers the global ValidationFilter, and exposes API docs. It is the one place that knows every layer, which is why the Api project is allowed to reference Infrastructure.
tour.languageLesson: ASP.NET Core extension methods on IServiceCollection, such as services.AddApplication(), let each project register its own services. Program.cs stays short, and each layer owns its wiring.

tour.title: Domain: Users and Tenancy
tour.description: The Domain layer holds the framework-free core model. User is the most depended-upon file in the graph. A User belongs to Organizations (the tenants) through OrganizationMembership, which carries an OrganizationRole. This membership model is the basis for the tenant isolation that AGENTS.md requires for every future resource, such as assistants, catalogs and conversations.

tour.title: Domain: Identity Records
tour.description: Authentication data is kept apart from the User entity. UserAccount records how a user signs in, such as a password credential or a Google provider account, so one User can have several login methods. EmailVerificationToken stores the single-use tokens behind the email verification flow. These two entities connect the tenancy model from Step 4 to the auth use cases that follow.

tour.title: Application Ports and Results
tour.description: The Application layer defines interfaces (ports) that Infrastructure must implement: repositories, a unit of work, token issuing, password hashing, email delivery and external identity validation. Use cases depend only on these abstractions, so the database, JWT library or email provider can be swapped out. Result.cs supplies a Result/error model, so expected failures are returned as values instead of thrown as exceptions.
tour.languageLesson: The Result pattern returns success or failure as a typed value, for example Result<T> with an Error. Callers must handle the failure case explicitly, and control flow stays visible, unlike exceptions used for routine validation outcomes.

tour.title: AuthService Use Cases
tour.description: AuthService is the main application service and one of the files with the most outgoing dependencies. It coordinates registration, login, Google sign-in, email verification, token refresh and logout, using only the ports from Step 6 and the entities from Steps 4-5. AuthErrors gathers the domain-specific failures it returns as Results. Following AGENTS.md, it is a plain service injected through DI, with no MediatR handlers.

tour.title: DTOs and Validation
tour.description: Request and response DTOs are the contract with the outside world, so EF entities are never exposed directly. AuthRequestValidators uses FluentValidation to check each incoming request. The Api's ValidationFilter runs those validators before a controller action executes, so invalid payloads are rejected early and in the same way everywhere.
tour.languageLesson: C# record types, such as public record LoginRequest(string Email, string Password), are concise, immutable and compared by value, which makes them a good fit for DTOs.

tour.title: AuthController and Endpoints
tour.description: AuthController is the thin HTTP surface over AuthService. It exposes /api/auth endpoints for register, login, google-session, verify-email, refresh and me (plus resend-verification and logout). Each action passes the request to the service and turns the Result into an HTTP status code, with no business logic or database access in the controller. Cortex.Api.http is a scratch file of sample requests for trying these endpoints by hand.

tour.title: Auth Integrations
tour.description: Infrastructure implements the ports from Steps 6-7 with real services. JwtTokenService issues short-lived access tokens and long-lived refresh tokens. BcryptPasswordHasher hashes passwords. GoogleIdentityTokenValidator verifies Google ID tokens. BrevoEmailService sends verification emails. Each adapter reads typed settings classes such as JwtSettings, so secrets come from configuration and are never hardcoded.
tour.languageLesson: The ASP.NET Core Options pattern binds a configuration section to a typed class, for example services.Configure<JwtSettings>(config.GetSection("Jwt")). Services then receive it through IOptions<T>, which gives strongly typed configuration that is easy to test.

tour.title: EF Core Persistence
tour.description: CortexDbContext is the EF Core gateway to PostgreSQL and the second most depended-upon file. Fluent configuration classes map each Domain entity to a table, which keeps persistence details out of the Domain layer. Repositories and UnitOfWork implement the Application interfaces, so AuthService can save changes without knowing EF Core exists.
tour.languageLesson: IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> classes hold the Fluent API mapping for each entity, and ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly loads them all at once. This keeps attributes off domain classes and keeps the DbContext small.

tour.title: Migrations and Database Tables
tour.description: EF Core migrations manage the database schema over time. InitialCreate builds the tenancy and identity tables: users, organizations, organization_memberships and user_accounts. A later migration adds email_verification_tokens for the verification flow. Each table mirrors an entity from Steps 4-5.
tour.languageLesson: EF Core migrations are generated C# classes with Up and Down methods. They apply schema changes in order and can be reversed. A design-time DbContext factory lets the dotnet ef tooling create the context without starting the whole application.

tour.title: Configuration and Settings
tour.description: appsettings.json and its Development override provide the sections that bind to the settings classes from Step 10: JWT, Google, Brevo and Frontend. .env.example lists the environment variables needed to run locally, so real secrets stay out of source control. launchSettings.json sets up local run profiles.

tour.title: Containerization
tour.description: The Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build: a build stage compiles and publishes the .NET solution, and a runtime stage keeps only the published output. docker-compose.yml runs the api service with its environment. .dockerignore keeps local artifacts out of the build context.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use several FROM statements. The SDK image compiles the app, and the smaller ASP.NET runtime image ships it, so build tools are left out of the production image.

tour.title: Frontend Integration Contract
tour.description: FRONTEND_INTEGRATION.md describes how the planned Next.js frontend with NextAuth v5 will use the auth endpoints from Step 9. It covers exchanging credentials or a Google ID token for the backend's JWT pair, refreshing access tokens, and handling email verification links. It ties the backend auth flow you have just followed to the user-facing experience.
